newsitem.title: USA: New fund labels reduce guesswork.
newsitem.headline: New fund labels reduce guesswork.

text.p: When you set out to assemble a portfolio of mutual funds that can meet your financial goals, it's important to choose funds that cover a variety of different types of investments.
That way, you won't suffer too much if one sector of the financial markets loses ground.

Until recently, choosing the right mix of funds has been a confusing process -- in part because many fund names are misleading. But a new system introduced by Morningstar Mutual Funds in Chicago should help solve the problem. Already, it has changed the way many people talk about mutual funds.

Many funds have been lumped into confusing categories such as "growth", "aggressive growth", or "equity income." Funds often use such phrases in their names -- for example, T. Rowe Price Equity Income or AIM Aggressive Growth.

Trouble is, no one is quite sure what terms like "equity income" or "aggressive growth" mean. As a result, two funds with very different investment styles might fall into the same category. For example, Fidelity Value, which invests in undervalued securities of large companies, falls into the same "growth" category as Janus Enterprise, which invests in small, fast-growing companies.

Alternatively, two funds with the same investment styles might be classified in different categories -- with dangerous results. Take Babson Enterprise, which invests in neglected shares of small companies and is classified as a small-company fund. Royce Equity-Income also invests in shares of small companies, but it is classified as an Equity-Income fund.

An investor who put money in both funds might assume that she was getting two very different funds, thus gaining the benefits of diversification among different market sectors. In fact, the investor is getting a double dose of the out-of-favour small company stocks both funds buy.

The new Morningstar system changes all that. It eliminates five domestic stock fund categories based on stated investment objectives -- aggressive growth, equity income, growth, growth and income, or small company -- and replaces them with categories that reflect a fund's actual holdings.

Each fund will have a two-part identity. The first is based on the size of the companies whose shares the fund typically holds: small, medium or large. The second part reflects the fund's investment style -- whether it tends to hold growth stocks, value stocks or a mix of the two.

Funds that take a growth-oriented approach to stock-picking are willing to pay premium prices for shares of companies that can deliver above-average earnings growth over time. Funds that take a value approach tend to buy neglected shares of firms with modest or unrecognized growth prospects. Still other funds blend both growth and value stocks in their portfolio.
That may sound complex, but it makes investing in funds much simpler.

For example, Morningstar used to classify Parnassus Fund as a "growth" fund. Now, it will be known as a "Small Value" fund. The fund's investment objective may still be capital gains -- or "growth" -- but its new category tells investors more about what the fund buys in its pursuit of that goal.

Now an investor who owns Parnassus knows that through the fund he owns neglected shares of small companies. He also knows that the fund's performance should be compared to funds that hold similar stocks.
In the past, an investor might have compared Parnassus' returns to those of other "growth" funds that had quite different portfolios.

What's more, an investor seeking to build a diversified portfolio can use the new classification system to find funds that offer a stake in all of the major stock categories. For example, such a portfolio might include a large blend fund, a small blend fund and a medium blend fund. That would create a portfolio that included growth and value stocks of every size.
The new system also introduces sensible categories for international and bond funds. Thus, you can use it to assemble a portfolio that's broadly diversified in those markets as well.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
